subject: biology-hl
topicLabel: C1.2 — Cell respiration & D1.2 — Protein synthesis (Feb–Mar unit)

items.stem: ATP is described as the universal energy currency because it:
choices: Stores large amounts of energy for long periods
Releases small, manageable amounts of energy when hydrolysed to ADP + phosphate
Is only produced in muscle cells
items.note: ATP hydrolysis releases a small packet of energy usable by every cell — unlike one big glucose burn. Universal: all life uses ATP.

items.stem: The overall equation for aerobic respiration is:
items.note: Same equation as photosynthesis reversed. Option 1 is anaerobic in animals; option 4 is anaerobic in yeast.

items.stem: Where do glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation occur?
items.note: Location questions are near-guaranteed: glycolysis in the cytoplasm (before mitochondria evolved), Krebs in the matrix, ETC on the inner membrane.

items.stem: Glycolysis produces:
choices: 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP and 2 NADH from one glucose
items.note: Glucose (6C) split into 2 pyruvate (3C). 4 ATP produced, 2 invested → net 2. Works without oxygen.

items.stem: The role of oxygen in aerobic respiration is to:
choices: Act as the terminal electron acceptor at the end of the ETC, forming water
items.note: Oxygen combines with electrons and H⁻ at ETC's end → water. Without O₂ the ETC backs up and only anaerobic respiration continues.

items.stem: In anaerobic respiration in human muscle, pyruvate is converted to:
items.note: Animals: lactate (muscle fatigue). Yeast/plants: ethanol + CO₂ (fermentation). Both regenerate NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue.

items.stem: Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy than aerobic respiration because:
choices: Glucose is not fully oxidized — much energy remains in lactate/ethanol
items.note: Only glycolysis runs (≈ 2 ATP). Lactate/ethanol still contain most of glucose's original energy.

items.stem: In a respirometer with potassium hydroxide solution added, the pressure change measures:
choices: O₂ consumption (KOH absorbs the CO₂ produced)
items.note: KOH removes CO₂, so the only gas change is O₂ decrease → fluid moves toward the organism. Controls: same temperature (water bath), same volume.

items.stem: Chemiosmosis in oxidative phosphorylation refers to:
choices: Protons pumped into the intermembrane space flowing back through ATP synthase
items.note: ETC pumps H⁻ into the intermembrane space; the gradient drives ATP synthase. That's why cristae (surface area) matter.

items.stem: NADH and FADH₂ produced in respiration:
choices: Carry electrons and hydrogen to the electron transport chain
items.note: Hydrogen carriers (NADH from glycolysis/Krebs, FADH₂ from Krebs) deliver electrons to the ETC — where oxidative phosphorylation happens.

items.stem: The correct sequence for gene expression is:
choices: Transcription (DNA → mRNA) in the nucleus, then translation (mRNA → protein) at ribosomes
Translation in the nucleus, then transcription
items.note: Eukaryotes: transcription in the nucleus, mRNA exits via pores, translation at ribosomes (free or on rough ER).

items.stem: Which enzyme unwinds DNA and joins RNA nucleotides during transcription?
items.note: RNA polymerase does both jobs along the template strand, starting at the promoter and moving 3′ → 5′ to build mRNA 5′ → 3′.

items.stem: One difference between RNA and DNA is that RNA:
choices: Contains ribose and uracil instead of deoxyribose and thymine
items.note: RNA: ribose sugar, uracil pairs with adenine, usually single-stranded. DNA: deoxyribose, thymine, double helix.

items.stem: A sequence of three mRNA bases coding for one amino acid is a:
items.note: mRNA: codon. tRNA: anticodon. DNA: triplet. Three related words — exams test that you use the right one.

items.stem: The genetic code is described as universal and degenerate. This means:
choices: The same codons specify the same amino acids in nearly all organisms; several codons can code for the same amino acid
Each codon codes for many amino acids
Every organism has a different code
items.note: Universality is why a human gene can be expressed in bacteria (GMO insulin). Degeneracy also buffers point mutations.

items.stem: During translation, the anticodon of tRNA pairs with:
items.note: tRNA: one end carries a specific amino acid; the anticodon loop base-pairs with the mRNA codon in the ribosome.

items.stem: Peptide bonds between amino acids are formed:
choices: In the ribosome as the polypeptide grows during translation
items.note: The ribosome catalyses peptide bonds between successive amino acids delivered by tRNAs.

items.stem: In eukaryotes, the mRNA that leaves the nucleus has had its introns removed by:
items.note: Pre-mRNA contains introns (non-coding) and exons (coding): splicing removes introns, joining exons into mature mRNA. (Bacterial mRNA needs no splicing.)

items.stem: The start codon AUG codes for:
choices: Methionine — it also signals the start of translation
items.note: AUG = methionine/start. Stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) do not code for an amino acid — they release the polypeptide.

items.stem: A respirometer contains a small mammal and KOH solution in a sealed chamber at constant temperature in a water bath. Explain what the movement of the fluid towards the chamber shows, and why temperature control is essential.
markscheme: Respiration consumes O₂ and produces CO₂ (1)
KOH absorbs the CO₂, so the only gas change is O₂ decrease (1)
Decreased gas volume/pressure → fluid moves towards the chamber → rate of movement = O₂ consumption rate (1)
Temperature control: respiration rate depends on enzyme activity; without it, gas expansion from heat would confound the O₂ measurement (1)
items.tactic: Respirometer questions: KOH's job, the direction of movement, and the two controls (temperature, equal volume) — all three are commonly examined.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of tRNA allows it to fulfil its role in translation.
markscheme: Cloverleaf shape held by base pairing — compact carrier (1)
Anticodon: three bases complementary to a specific mRNA codon → ensures the right amino acid is placed (1)
3′ end binds one specific amino acid, attached by an activating enzyme (1)
Delivers amino acids to the ribosome in the sequence dictated by mRNA codons (1)
items.tactic: Structure–function answer: anticodon pairs with codon (specificity) + amino acid binding site (delivery) + shape. Named parts, not vague 'it helps'.
